newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Chretien pledges to reverse spending cuts.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Chretien pledges to reverse spending cuts.

text.p: Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien on Monday launched the first full day of his re-election campaign by pledging to loosen the government's purse strings.

With his budget-slashing Finance Minister Paul Martin at his side, Chretien told a news conference in Halifax that he would reverse planned spending cuts in the next fiscal year because of the government's success in cutting its deficit.

"Because we are ahead of schedule on deficit reduction, we can now afford to reinvest in the health care system without jeopardising our deficit targets," declared Chretien, who came to power in late 1993 on a promise of "jobs, jobs, jobs" but was soon forced to engage in budget cuts to salvage Canada's standing in financial markets.

Much of the budget axe fell on health and social payments to the provinces. Monday's announcement would restore some of the planned cuts if the Liberals are re-elected in the June 2 federal polls, as current surveys suggest they will be.

Chretien pledged to add C$700 million (U.S. $500 million) to next year's planned cash transfers under the Canada Health and Social Transfer (CHST), the block fund transfer to the provinces. His government had cut the CHST cash transfers from C$19.3 billion ($13.8 billion) in 1994-95 to C$12.5 billion ($8.9 billion) in the current fiscal year.

It had been scheduled to decline to C$11.8 billion ($8.4 billion) in 1998-99 but now will stay at this year's level as a new floor, thereby avoiding even deeper cuts that had been planned for future years.

The government's health programme is a sacred cow in Canada, and Chretien's announcement immediately drew the scorn of his rivals on both the right and left, as well as a thumbs-down from the financial markets.
Leftist New Democratic Party (NDP) leader Alexa McDonough said in Vancouver that voters would not be tricked.

"They're not going to be fooled into thinking that a government that steals your purse like a petty thief and then offers you bus fare to get home at the end of the day is actually addressing your needs," she told a news conference organised by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC).

Conservative Party leader Jean Charest told a similar news conference: "They cut cash transfers 40 percent, they did this without any consultation, they did it unilaterally and without any kind of a plan."
The Reform Party, vying with the Conservatives for the right-wing vote, said Chretien had pledged in a debate in 1993 not to touch health spending.
But Chretien said: "Our deficit reduction efforts have been far more successful than anyone could have predicted because of a stronger economy and low interest rates."

Martin told Reuters the deficit for 1996-97 could be under C$16 billion ($11.4 billion), well under the C$24.3 billion ($17.3 billion) originally planned and the "no more than C$19 billion ($13.6 billion)" prediction he had given in February.
The Canadian dollar, already near two-year lows because of reluctance by the Bank of Canada to match U.S. interest rate increases, slipped further on the Chretien announcement.

The Liberals have been leading by margins ranging from 24 to 40 points among decided voters in recent national polls, although Canadian voters have proved volatile in recent years and around one-third tell pollsters they are undecided.

A poll released on Monday night by the CBC gave the Liberals 42 percent among decided voters to 20 percent for the Conservatives, 15 percent for Reform, 11 percent for the NDP and eight percent for the separatist Bloc Quebecois.

But the CBC said half of the Liberal and Conservative supporters said they could change their mind, implying room for big swings in public opinion. The poll was taken April 17 to 22 among 2,541 voters, with a margin of error of two percentage points 19 times out of 20.
